utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you'd like to take a seat. Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I begin the examination of this witness, there is a small administrative matter I'd ask to go into private session to address with the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, pursuant to an order of the Trial Chamber dated the 13th of July, 2003, granting the Prosecution's application for the admission of B-1054 -- I'm sorry, the 30th of July, 2003, granting the Prosecution's application for the admission of B-1054's testimony from the trial of Prosecutor versus Mitar Vasiljevic, case number 98-32, the Prosecution would like to formally tender one binder containing the transcripts and related exhibits comprising the evidence of B-1054. I would note that tabs 2, 7, 8, and 9 of that binder were exhibits that were placed under seal in the previous trial and would ask that that protection be continued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, the binder will get the next exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit 522, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: May I ask to begin by requesting that the witness be shown tab 2 of that binder. It is the pseudonym sheet from the prior proceeding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: B-1054, is that your name contained on this sheet of paper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. 1054, the Chamber is in possession of your testimony and exhibits from your prior testimony from the Vasiljevic trial. I will not ask you to repeat that testimony. I would like to ask you to clarify in part and summarise some of the more significant aspects of that evidence. Your sworn testimony reveals that on the 10th of June, 1992, there was fighting in your village, the village of Koritnik, just north of the town of Visegrad at the homes of a number of Muslim residents in that village was fired upon. Shortly after the fighting, Serb neighbours of yours delivered a message to you and other Muslim members of your community. Can I ask you to tell the Chamber what that message was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: The message was that we should leave our village because our [redacted], told us that there was ethnic cleansing and that we had to move out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your testimony continues with you and most of the Muslims from your village gathering the next day with as many of your possessions as you could carry and leaving the village toward the town of Visegrad. You went on further to describe an encounter at a crossroads during which several armed Serbs discussed whether to kill you there or in the town itself. You went on to testify that you arrived in the town at around 3.00 to 4.00 in the afternoon, and after trying to go to the Red Cross, you and the others congregated in front of the Hotel Visegrad. You went on to describe how after approximately an hour, you were instructed to go to Pionirska Street in a now empty Muslim part of the town itself. You testified to eventually arriving and taking refuge in the abandoned house of Mr. Memic. I want to now ask you several questions regarding what happened in the Memic house. Can I ask you to begin by telling us how many people were in this group and what was its composition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: When we moved from the new hotel, when a Serb policeman told us to go to Pionirska Street, we arrived in front of Memic's house. There was a group of some 70 people, mostly elderly men and children and young girls. We were wet from the rain. We changed. Somebody had tea, somebody had coffee. And in the meantime, Mitar Vasiljevic and Milan Lukic arrived, as well as Sredoje Lukic and Milan Susnjar, also known as Laco, and they told us to go to one room. Then Milan Lukic put a cloth on the table telling us to put all our jewellery on that cloth. We did that, and then we were forced into another room where Milan Susnjar was, and he stripped us naked. We had to dance. They were giving instruction, move forward, move backward. Skip this way and that. After that, we put our clothes on. And then they took out Jasmina Kurspahic, and Jasmina Vila. I don't know where they took them. When we asked them what happened, they wouldn't tell us anything when they came back as to what had happened to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when the group was forced to move from this house to a house very close by, to a house owned by a family by the of name Omeragic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: After that, when they took all this from us and mistreated us, then they -- then Milan Lukic who was standing at the door of Jusuf Memic's house, and Vasiljevic at the other house, and then we were escorted to Omer Memic's house. And at the end, we were burned shortly after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe what happened in the Omeragic house.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: When we reached this Omeragic house, the carpets had been -- some oil or fuel had been poured on the carpets. And that is when they set fire to us. Amongst us was a two-day-old baby. The children were screaming. The women, the old men, were trying to help. I was right next to the window, and I threw out my 13-year-old son out the window, and then I followed him a couple of minutes later. Then I was wounded in my left arm and left leg. I went into the stream and the sewage canal where I stayed for three nights and three days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From where you were in the sewage canal, could you see what happened to the people in the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: It wasn't far. It was about 50 metres away so that I heard screams, cries for help. It was unbearable. When I think about it, I start dreaming. I feel distressed and awful. It was terrible. It was painful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people are you -- can you estimate for us how many people died in the house that night.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: There was us from our village, and others from the neighbouring villages, so there were about 70 of us. And then there were people already in that house when we arrived, so there may have been 75, maybe even more. I didn't count those people that were already there when we arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many members of your immediate family died that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Six of my family members died. My mother-in-law and onwards from that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you threw your son out of the window of that house, did you know whether or not he had survived the events of that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: I didn't know. I had no contact with him for five years. We met five years later in Zenica. And this was a terrible experience and a shock to see him five years later. We had parted when he was only 13 and a half.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your son know that you had survived that night during the course of that five years?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: No, he didn't know. He didn't know anything about me, nor did I know anything about him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please briefly describe to the Chamber the injuries you sustained that night.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: That night, while I was in the sewage canal, there were worms all over my wounds. I had wounds in my left arm and leg. When I reached the Gorazde hospital, I was in a sorry state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally after escaping from Visegrad, did you learn that this group had perpetrated a similar crime to another group of Muslim civilians in a house in Visegrad, without going into the detail of that event?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Yes, at the Bikavac, about 80 people were burnt by this same group. Again, these were civilians, elderly people and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions. If the Chamber will recall, Mr. Milosevic sought to ask an earlier witness some questions about Visegrad, in particular, the event of Murat Sabanovic and his threats to blow up a dam. The third witness today is the witness that the Prosecution has brought who has personal knowledge of those events. This witness doesn't, so perhaps that will save some time on the examination of this witness. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you hear what counsel says. This witness does not know about the events you were asking the other witness about. However, there is a witness coming shortly who you can ask about those events. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that the witness has no knowledge about what Mr. Groome referred to. But the witness mentions in her statement the presence of certain units of the Uzice Corps, and this presence is linked to those events. So I will ask the witness indirectly something with regard to the event that Mr. Groome mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So Witness 1054, you gave two statements to the investigators of the Tribunal, on the 12th and 13th of February, 1998. That is the first one. And the second one on the 15th of June, 2000. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In addition to these statements, you also gave a statement to the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the centre of security services in Zenica on the 14th of August, 1995 which was three years prior to this other first statement. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: I didn't give any statements in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It doesn't matter whether you made them in Zenica, but representatives of that centre in Zenica took a statement from you. I have that statement here, which you signed. [redacted]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Madam 1054, would you be kind enough to have a look at this statement, please, and to give it back to me because I have some questions to put to you about it. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have several copies of that statement, to avoid it going from one hand to another. It was received from the Prosecution, and I prepared it for my own benefit, for my own questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness have the copy in front of her. Are there any English translations for us?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I've just sent for them, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness B-1054, just have a look at that document. It's suggested that that's a statement which you made to -- I forget. I think it was the investigation centre in Zenica. Do you recognise it now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is my signature, but I don't remember making a statement to anyone in Zenica. In 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Madam 1054, the fact that it says the centre in Zenica doesn't mean that you were taken to Zenica to make that statement. Probably an official person from that centre came to take the statement from you, and those officials persons are indicated. It says: "Statement taken by authorised official persons" and there are two signatures. The record taker and your own signature. "Statement given by Witness 1054," that is your full first and last name, and you confirm it with your signature. Isn't that so? Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the signature is mine. But really for me to make a statement in 1995, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not claiming, nor could I know technically, how this happened, whether they took you to Zenica or whether someone came to take the statement from you because this is a large area. I just wanted to establish whether this is your signature. So let's move on so as not to waste any more time, as I'm sure my time will be limited. On page 2 of your statement of the 12th of February, 1998, in the third paragraph, I'm talking about the statement to the investigators, you say that tensions in Visegrad could be felt as early as 1991, that barricades were set up, and that the fighting started in 1992. Is that right, Madam 1054?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, who was erecting these barricades and who was fighting who in Visegrad and the environs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: The barricades were erected by our neighbour Serbs so that we couldn't go into town or leave, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me who the fighting was between.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Our neighbouring Serbs attacked our Muslim villages thinking that they would frighten us and force us to leave our own homes. They started looting and taking things away. We were attacked as Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But when you say "fighting" that implies two sides.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Fighting, meaning that the Serb side consists of those neighbours of ours who armed themselves, and they attacked us. Yes, it is basically two sides, but it is the case of neighbours attacking us who were innocent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Groome mentioned that I should not ask you anything about other events, but do you have any knowledge at all as to who are Murat Sabanovic and Avdija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Well, they are people like any other people. Not animals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That much I can surmise myself.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: They were men, and they had to fight to pull out the people who were left stranded on the other bank of the Drina. We had no choice except to get out, otherwise we would have been killed. We were forced by circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did they help you get out of there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: They didn't help us, but they fought to pull us out. The entire parish, which includes over 50 villages with Muslim population, there were only Muslim houses and a couple of Croat houses. There were no Serbs there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Except this Murat and Avdija Sabanovic who fought to pull you out, how many other men were there with them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: They were not fighting with rifles. They were fighting to pull us out of there. They didn't have weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they didn't have weapons.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: They didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know apart from them, and you obviously know them, do you know Nedzad and Ibrahim Dervisevic, and Jasim Ferid [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Zakija Jamuk [phoen] and Medo Kulovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Duro Subasic [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: I don't know him either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, and in fact you confirmed you knew the Sabanovic brothers, that in July 1991, they destroyed the monument Ivo Andric?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: I wasn't in Visegrad then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't hear about the destruction of the Ivo Andric monument?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Ivo Andric was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: It was a monument to one man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that man whose monument was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: It was a great man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the relevance of this to the burning of civilians in a house? 70 of them. Are you saying there was a provocation of some sort, Mr. Milosevic? Otherwise, I cannot see what relevance it has.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, in any case, the destruction of the monument of Ivo Andric, who is a writer, and the only Yugoslav Nobel prizewinner, a Serb, falls within the context of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And this has to do with the context of events which were taking place throughout that time. And if it cannot certainly justify burning people inside a house, or any other crime, but it helps understand the context of facts, the context of mutual conflict based along ethnic lines because the monument Ivo Andric was destroyed because Ivo Andric was a Serb, not because of any other of his qualities. He, as I said, was the only Nobel Prize winner in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That may or may not be so. But the difficulty is this witness's evidence deals with a specific event. If you've got questions about that, she can no doubt answer them and deal with it as best she can. But to ask her generally about tensions in the area doesn't seem to me to assist your case. No doubt there were tensions in the area. But it's no defence to this kind of action which we're dealing with. That's the difficulty, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I don't even think that I have anything to defend myself from here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. 1054, what does this event have to do with Serbia at all? Was anyone from Serbia involved in this event?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Well, our Serb neighbours were involved. They attacked us. I didn't say that anybody from Serbia had come. It was our Serb neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So Serbia is involved in the sense that those neighbours of yours were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not for the witness to answer. It may be a matter that we have to deal with in due course. All the witness can say, and you can ask her about this, is who was involved. And she tells you that the Serb neighbours were involved.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But since the witness, and I have to ask her this, Mr. May, regardless of the fact that you want to limit things to only one event from this entire context, the witness says that before the attack on the village, some units of the Uzice Corps had been in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You did mention that, Ms. 1054, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Well, certainly Uzice troops had been in Visegrad, and they had entered in full military equipment. I didn't say that it was them who had set us on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I wanted to ask you, do you know that it was precisely this Murat Sabanovic, whom you know, and a large group together with him had occupied the plant of the Visegrad hydro power station? It was in all the papers, and you could have heard in public this conversation in which they threatened to blow up the hydro power station, which would have caused a tragedy in that whole area, both on the side that belongs to Bosnia and Herzegovina and on the bank that belongs to Serbia, involving a large number of Muslim and Serb villages. It would have caused a natural, I would say, disaster with unfathomable consequences. It would have caused the destruction of the dam and everything behind that dam.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: That is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Okay, then. I wanted to ask you, because this actually happened and we had the opportunity to hear the conversation between this man and his superiors in Sarajevo, I wanted to ask you do you know that the army had come there to restore order and to prevent the tragedy that would have taken the lives of thousands?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: It's not true the army had come to restore order. They had only misled people to return, people who had fled, and many more people eventually suffered. As for this conversation between this Sabanovic and others, I wasn't there. I don't know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You just said when the army came, people returned.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Yes, there were a lot of people who had fled from the environs of the town. And when the army came, they addressed people over the public-address system, and they said "it's safe." And people had come back, but later Drina was full of bodies floating in it and red with blood.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is not true. The Uzice Corps said everybody was safe as long as we are here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Well, that is not true. There are other people who can discuss it with you. Whether it was safe or not, I'm not in a position to say to you. I'm not in a position to say why they had come.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know that they had come to restore normality, normalcy, normal relations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: I don't know about that. Somebody who is more familiar with the details will be able to tell you, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you do say very precisely in your statement: "My village" - this is paragraph 4 at the beginning of the statement - "my village was attacked by my own neighbours, not the Uzice Corps."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: I never said the Uzice Corps had attacked us. But they were involved with our names, the Serbs who lived with us together in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean to say there were units of the Uzice Corps in the area of Visegrad, then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Yes. They must have come from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you don't understand why they were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: I don't understand. Somebody else will explain it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have information about any crime whatsoever committed by any member of the Uzice Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: I don't have such information. Maybe somebody else does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm asking you. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: No, I can't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Fine. But you said here that it was your neighbours who attacked you. I suppose you know all their names, names of all these neighbours who launched this attack on your village.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Do you want me to list them?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Not now. We'll come to that. You say in paragraph 6 on page 2 of the statement that "all the young men left the village before the attack and fled to the woods."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Yes. They had to hide, lest they be taken alive and tortured.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. They ran into the woods. Did they know that there would be an attack and hid beforehand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: No, they were fleeing from the attack, and they were followed by a storm of bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about Ahmed Sejdic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did you hear anything at all about these Muslim barricades and the mobilisation of residents, including from your village, under his command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Nothing at all. I don't see your husband mentioned anywhere in your statement. I don't want to mention his name because you are a protected witness, lest I identify you. Did he hide in the woods together with the other men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Yes, he did, but you shouldn't think that they had any weapons. They were bare-handed. They had no weapons at all. They were hiding from a storm of bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me: During the attack on your village on the 10th of June, the attack being mounted by your neighbours, did any of the residents get killed or wounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: You mean the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm talking about the attack on your village. You said your village was attacked on the 10th of June?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was anybody hurt then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Nobody was hurt, but they did storm the village. They asked where the men were, and they started looting immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know those men who came and started looting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Of course I know them. They had lived with us in the same village for decades. Of course I know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were they from your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Yes, because Koritnik was next to a Serb village. There were Serbs and Muslims living next to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand that these Serb neighbours who took part in that attack were looking for the men from your village. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many people lived in Koritnik before the outbreak of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: I didn't count them. I know there were 80 houses populated by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many men left the village before the attack, before the 10th of June?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Well, they wouldn't have fled at all if it hadn't been for another neighbour from another village who came crying to our village saying: "Please, run away, dear neighbours. If you are caught alive, you will be killed." I don't want to name the person. I don't want him to come to any harm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not even asking you to name this neighbour who tried to help you. You mentioned in closed session at the beginning that a certain Grujic, Dusan Grujic, had come and told you that ethnic cleansing was going on and that you should hide.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did he use those words, "We are carrying out ethnic cleansing and you should run for cover"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right, Ms. 1054. On page 2, paragraph 8, you said that two or three days later, the soldiers came back and surrounded the village. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Yes, they surrounded it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said two or three days later, they came back and surrounded the village.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: They didn't surround it. They came to tell us that we should move out of our houses. They came right to the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I only wanted to remind you. You say: "Two or three days later, the soldiers came back and surrounded the village. They told us again we had to surrender our weapons, and the men had to surrender." On that occasion, the following people came to the village, and you enumerate, Milorad Lipovac, Ciro, and Dusan Grujic. Dusan said that ethnic cleansing was being carried out and we had to leave. He said he would take us to Kladanj and put us up there, that we should take a supply of food for two days. We were not verbally or physically abused. So they had come back after the attack because you say it was two or three days later.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: You've just asked me that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking this because in the transcript of your testimony mentioned by Mr. Groome, you were asked by their side whether the people who had mounted the attack had come back two or three days later. And on page 1423 of the transcript, you replied: "They never came back to the village. They did not dare to come back." That's what you said. And it says so in the transcript. So tell me now what is the truth? What it says in your statement about their coming back or what you testified to, as I quoted, from the transcript, that they never came back and they did not dare to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. The transcript goes on: "Did there come a time when soldiers came back and surrounded the village?" "They came looking again, but we were hiding in the woods." "Did there come a time when you were told that you had to leave the village?" And so it goes on. So that's the complete passage from the transcript. Yes, Witness 1054, do you want to add anything to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Regardless of whether they came back or not, tell me what was it they were looting, because you stated previously that the village had been looted earlier on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Everything they could get out, they did get out of the houses. They also took away the cattle right in front of us. They boarded it on tractors, TV sets and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But you said before that in your statement that previously the village had been looted. So how could they loot it twice then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: It wasn't twice. It was once as we were getting ready to go. When this neighbour, Dusan Grujic came and told us there would be ethnic cleansing, they came on the same day with tractors and took our stuff on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there any looting before that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: No, not before that. There was intimidation. They wanted to scare us. They wanted to make us leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So before that, there was no looting, is that right, Ms. 1054?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Yeah, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why did you write in your statement, then, and this in paragraph 3 of your statement: "Before the attack in my village, the Uzice Corps was there, and they were looting and plundering. I can't be precise about the dates, but they were there before the 10th of June, 1992." Why did you accuse the soldiers of the Uzice Corps of having looted your village when you said that later on it was these people who looted your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: I said a few minutes ago, as far as the looting of the Uzice Corps is concerned, there are other people who can explain this a bit better than I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But I'm reading your very own statement, not this other person who can explain it a bit better. So what you wrote down here that they looted you and plundered, people from the Uzice Corps, before the 10th of June, so that's not true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: It is true, and it will be known, when they came, what they did, and everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But that does not match what you're saying now when you say that they came after the 10th of June, and that's when they plundered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has answered that matter. Yes, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the second page, the person you mentioned who said to you - I wrote it down - Dusan Grujic, that ethnic cleansing was being carried out, and then you say that he told you that you were supposed to go. Did he wear some kind of a uniform then or did he wear civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Yes, it was a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, so he wore a uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when he said this to you, that this was ethnic cleansing, did you understand what this was all about? Did you know what ethnic cleansing was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Well, as far as I could understand it, and all of us who were present there, of course, ethnic cleansing meant that we should not exist there at all and that we should not live together the way we lived beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see. So that's the word he used, this is the expression he used, that they would carry out ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Well, I guess I did not invent it. I think that's exactly what he said, that word.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But they did not mistreat you or abuse you when they said then there would be ethnic cleansing. Nobody mistreated you or abused you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Well, no. He and Milorad Lipovac who came with him, the two of them didn't. But then we paid with our very own skins when we went down to town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about that event now, I'm asking you about this: So nobody touched you and that's what they said to you, that's what you're saying and you say that they told you that ethnic cleansing was being carried out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Yes, and Aisa Kurspahic gave him the keys to her house. He said: "You'll give me the keys to your house".

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you obeyed them and the next morning you left the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Yes, of course you had to obey. We left under duress. I mean, who would have left his own home and everything he had unless it was under duress? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They were not forcing, they were not mistreating you, they were not threatening you, they were not shooting anyone, they were not beating anyone? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Well, that day there was no shooting, of course there wasn't any shooting on that day, but they did attack before that and you had to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did you inform your husband in any way that you were leaving your house and that you were going?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Why would I inform my husband when they informed us, our neighbours did. They informed all of us that we all had to go. It wasn't information on an individual basis, we were all told that we had to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see your husband at all from the moment when this attack took place, the attack on Koritnik and when you left the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Of course we saw him. Everybody in the village was in their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, so they returned. First they escaped to the woods, and then they returned after the attack? Is that right, Mrs. 1054?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Yeah, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: In this statement of yours, the one you gave to the police, the one we showed here a short while ago, you do not mention anywhere that an attack was launched on Koritnik on the 10th of June; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: I don't mention it; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Well, can't you see that you're reading it yourself, it's right in front of you, that there was an attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But I'm saying that in this statement that you gave in 1995, there is no mention of an attack on Koritnik, you say: "A few local Serbs came, Lipovac Milorad, Grujic Dusan, and Milorad Djuric," and you say that they informed you that you had to move out. That is what is written here in that statement of yours. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Yes. So what do you want now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in your statement given to the investigators, you do not mention a Dusan Djuric; you mention Dusan Grujic and Ciro Grujic. Whereas here in this statement, you talk about Lipovac Milorad, Djuric Dusan, and Milorad Djuric. So you mention completely different names in the two different statements --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: To be fair to the witness, she mentions one particular name, and she has mentioned it today. Whether it assists anyone to have this sort of detail is a matter, of course, for the Trial Chamber. What she says in her statement - and I'm looking at the statement of the 12th and 13th of February - was that she was not at home when the village was attacked, and then she describes what happened. Then she said: Two or three days later, soldiers came back. They had to surrender, and they were told to leave the village. And the man that she mentioned said there was ethnic cleansing and they had to go. Now, that was her account then. And whether it assists to have the precise detail as to the date, of course, must be doubtful. This was over ten years. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I really don't want to hold it against you, the fact that you don't know the Serbian language, because the assumption is that you don't have to know the language. But in the statement that I am quoting, she talks about Dusan Djuric and Milorad Djuric nicknamed Cinda. That's how the statement starts. And he informed them about the ethnic cleansing. But in the statement she gave to the investigators, she talks about Grujic. These are two completely different surnames. Djuric starts with a D-J, and so on and so forth, and Grujic starts with different letters, so you can see it exactly here. Nowhere in this statement does she mention the same persons. She talks about completely different persons. And her testimony is that these men came. So this is not a marginal matter; this is a question of credibility, of accuracy of this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There may be difficulties about the translation, but the English translation gives the name which she has mentioned throughout. Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not have a translation of the Zenica statement. I can have that done on an emergency basis and have it to the Court on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I was referring to the witness statement which was taken by the Prosecution which refers to that man. But certainly we should have the Zenica statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just point out, given the traumatic events that followed this event, the fire and everything else, it seems somewhat --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Academic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- academic to remember the precise names of all of the people in the events preceding it, but I'll leave that to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will have a copy of that statement exhibited, and we'll have to determine in the context of all the evidence the significance of that discrepancy.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wish to have the point understood: Completely different names are mentioned in this statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, of course, Mr. Milosevic. It's not going to be one and the same man all the time because it wasn't one and the same man who came to our village all the time to mistreat us and to force us to leave our homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, all right. If that's the explanation, then we can go on, because you do not mention at all any Djurics or any person called Ciro. You mention a Thendo [phoen], and you say his name was Milorad Djuric; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Yes, well, Ciro is his nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Milorad Djuric Ciro, is that right? Is that who was there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Yes, he was there for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the statement given to the investigators, you say it was Dusan Grujic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Yes, Dusan Grujic came to tell us that there would be ethnic cleansing and that we had to leave. All of these people are neighbours. You don't have to persuade me of anything; I know them and I saw all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I don't want to deal with this any longer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because you said, Mr. May, that you are going to exhibit this statement so there is no need to discuss this with the witness any longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will get the exhibit number now for the statement. If we could have a copy handed in, please. Mr. Milosevic, have you got a copy of the statement to hand in, or maybe Mr. Tapuskovic has one. We'll leave one with the witness. It's all right, we have one for the Prosecution, we'll get the next --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have two more copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will get the next Defence exhibit number. We have one, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it will be 176. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And just for the record, in the preceding paragraph, the witness stated that Ciro is a nickname of Radomir Djuric.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just ask that the exhibit be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is important, actually, to see who it was who came to their village, who the people in their village were, because different names are referred to on different occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you came to Visegrad, you stayed -- you say that when you went to Visegrad, you first came across some Serbs who were wondering whether they should kill you or let you into Visegrad. That's what you said. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear the witness, her microphone is not on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the crossroads, you met some Serbs and they wondered whether they should let you go into Visegrad or whether they should kill you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness's microphone should be switched on. They are on now. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then nothing. They were debating whether they should kill you or not and then they let you enter town.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: They did not let us go. They would have killed us there and they would have thrown us into the Drina River, and they would have used that excavator. But Milorad Lipovac would not let them mistreat us. He said, "take them to town, and then -" begging your pardon - "fuck them any way you want."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, all right, Mrs. 1054. You stayed at the house of a certain Medic, or rather, first you were in one house and then another house, but that is not important; Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: One -- a group of us was in Jusuf Memic's house, and another group was in his son's house. And we were wet, we got caught in the rain, somebody had tea, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I heard that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: If you heard that, why are you asking me again?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you again about that. You mentioned that you had tea, et cetera, but I didn't ask you about that. And now you say that later they came, and you spoke about that here a few minutes ago. Milan Lukic, Sredoje Lukic, and Milan Susjnar, nicknamed Laco. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the statement you gave in Zenica in 1995, you mention that with them in the yard was a certain Bosko Djuric, a taxi driver. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Yes, for sure, he was there too while they were taking our money and our jewellery and gold, and they were stripping us, he was out there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why have you not mentioned him in this statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Well, I did mention him, but perhaps I got all confused because of everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I understand that explanation. But tell me, these people whose names you mentioned, did you know all of them personally; Milan Lukic, Sredoje Lukic, Susjnar, did you know them personally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: They are also our neighbours. Milan Susjnar lives down by Greben. When I went to work, I used to pass by his house. And Milan Lukic and Sredoje Lukic are from Rujiste. How could I not know them? I have lived in Visegrad for 40 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what were they professionally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Sredoje worked in the police, Sredoje Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he was a policeman?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in the events that you describe, was he still a policeman then or was he a civilian or did he wear some kind of a uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: At that time, he wore a uniform, a police uniform, but it wasn't the one that was worn beforehand. It was a dark one with some kind of little flags on the sleeve and on the cap.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So all three men you mentioned are persons you know well, and there can be no confusion regarding their identity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: There sure can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do they have anything to do with the Lukic who was suspected of the attack against civilians and their killing in Strbci?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Of course he does -- they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was it the same person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: It wasn't anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If that is one and the same man, do you know that in Serbia, he is a wanted person precisely on account of what had happened in Strbci, in connection with the crime in Strbci?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: I don't know whether he's wanted or not. I know that he is that man, that very man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. As far as I can remember, he was even arrested.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But in connection with the events in Strbci, as for what you're testifying about, that was not known at the time. In your statement, which you gave in 1995, you claim that Milan and Sredoje Lukic on that occasion raped Jasmina Zuban and Ifeta Kurspahic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: They took them away. The women came back in a terrible state; they were taking pills. They didn't rape them in my presence, so I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I just want to clear this up with you, Madam 1054, because there's a drastic difference. So please, look at the statement. You say, and I am quoting from the statement you gave to the police in Bosnia and Herzegovina: "The girls and women that they liked were raped, so they raped Ismeta Kurspahic and Zuban."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, there's nothing here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You go on to say that Lukic searched you in Jusuf Memic's house. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Yes, when he took our jewellery and money.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say in that statement that you handed over your money to him. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Yes, we all did; everything. He threw a cloth on the table and said, "Put all your jewellery and money here on the table."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement to the security centre, you mention that, too, don't you? How much money did he take from you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: He knows how much money he took. Anyway, the bag was full that he had collected from all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How much did you personally give him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: More than 2.000 German marks, apart from the jewellery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: However, during your testimony, you said that you handed over more than 2.000 German marks. But in your testimony for which we have the transcript, on page 1424, line 10 of the transcript, explaining what you had taken with you from the house when you left it on the 14th of June, you stated that you took some money and documents with you. Is that right? Where did all this jewellery come from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: We all had jewellery, not just me, and we all took it with us, of course. We didn't leave it behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In your statement to the investigators, on page 5, paragraph 2, you say that Lukic, about 2000 hours, took you to Adem Omeragic's house. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Yes, Milan Lukic, Sredoje Lukic, and Mitar Vasiljevic, they were there when we were forced from one house to the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And on page 2, paragraph 4 of the statement to the security centre in 1995, you say: "When we all entered, they shut the door, and then they came back with an incendiary material which started burning immediately." And you say that "Lukic fired a burst of fire into the ground at the exit so as to prevent the people from escaping."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Nobody could escape when there was a fire burning at the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, look at the statement that you gave three years later to the investigators. On page 6, paragraph 1, you say: "Some 30 minutes into our stay in that room, these two Lukics and Mitar Vasiljevic came back to this house. I saw them clearly. They did not enter the room, but they opened the door. And I saw Milan Lukic put a bomb on the floor, the kind that has a string attached to it, a fuse attached to it. The fire burns its way to the bomb, and then causes an explosion. I saw Milan Lukic holding the bomb in his hand. I saw him light the bomb at the door. And I saw him putting it down on the ground. People were sitting down. Lukic swore. I saw Sredoje and Mitar standing behind Milo Lukic. He was standing at the door."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: He wasn't. He was standing at the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: With reference to this same event, did you give a statement to Mustafa Sacirovic, known as Mule, that was later included in Naser Oric's book, "Srebrenica, Witnesses Accused? "

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: I don't know who this Mustafa is, nor do I know who Naser Oric is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But this is in tab 8. That I was given by Mr. Groome who was examining you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness have a copy.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know who tendered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was tendered under seal, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let the witness have a copy. What is it you want to ask the witness about here, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here, she says, and this is page 114 of the English version, 00816734, and I will shorten it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "First they lit something like gas at the door from which a flame started spreading to the room we were in." Was that how it was, Madam 1054?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Yes, of course it was. And as people started jumping out, two people - I don't want to name them - then they went under the window and they shot at the people through the window to prevent them from jumping out of the window.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you talking about a bomb with a fuse, yet here there's mention of a gas. You are confirming both. What was it? Can we establish what it was actually?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: The carpets in the room, they were already soaked with some sort of liquid, like oil or fuel or something. I didn't say it was gas, but the carpets on the floor were soaked in something so as to burn more quickly. And the bomb you mentioned was dropped in front of the door, not into the crowd.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How was this burning started? Was it with gas, as it says here, a bomb, or these soaked carpets? How did the fire start? Can we establish that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Milosevic, when something is sprinkled on the floor, it's sufficient to light a match. You know how this happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of course I do know when you soak something with gas, but you're talking about a bomb and a fuse.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Well, there was something else at the entrance, at the door, to kill the people, to prevent people from being able to escape through the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But in this statement to the security centre, you say that Lukic opened a burst of fire into the floor so as to prevent the people from fleeing, whereas in your statement to the investigators, you just say he had a bomb and the other two had rifles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: This device was dropped before a burst of fire was opened into the door. And when they shot at the window, it wasn't in a burst, but individual shots.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have to say to you that this sounds rather confusing to me because in your statement to the investigators, page 6, paragraph 2, you say that [redacted] jumped out of the window just when the bomb exploded. Is that right? So there was an explosion, not just burning but also a bomb that exploded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: I said a moment ago I didn't want to name who jumped out of the window, but you're still naming those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But the point here is for you to say that somebody jumped out of the window when there was an explosion. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So was there a bomb that exploded, or was there a gas, or was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. there carpet soaked and sprinkled with a liquid? What was it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think the witness has --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: What exploded? What went off?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just tell us again, once more for the benefit of the accused, what happened, and then we'll move on to a separate topic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the woman jumped out of the window, then I threw out my son as well. And two or three minutes later, I jumped out, too. I was wounded in my left arm and left leg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, before that, when the device was put in the room, and you've described the way in which the carpet had been sprinkled with some material or other, what happened when the device was put in the room. Just tell us briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The device was put in front of the door. And as the fuse was burning, eventually it exploded. Whereas there was fire spreading in the room, the carpet started burning. Just then, Lukic fired a burst, and then he was under the window while these people were jumping out to prevent the people from jumping out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but please, you explained that someone jumped out of the window, and as you say, you don't want to name those people, and just when the bomb went off. After that, you say, "While in those few minutes I was thinking what I should do, I was hit by a fragment in the leg, and I was burnt by the flame."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Yes, and on the hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How could a shrapnel hit you several minutes after the bomb exploded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: The shrapnel ricochetted probably from the rifle shot through the window, and then it flew through my leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So I see. That was the shrapnel that hit you three minutes after the bomb exploded, so it was a bullet that ricochetted, that came through the window and ricochetted from the wall. Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, under these circumstances, how could this witness possibly know the source of a piece of shrapnel that hit her in the leg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, this kind of detail is of no assistance, really. Mr. Milosevic, you've now had more than an hour and it's coming to time for an adjournment. We'll consider how long you should have. Are you asking for more time with this witness? Is there much more you want to ask her?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not much more. But I need a little more time, I do, Mr. May. And I agree with Mr. Groome that under such circumstances, it is difficult for anyone to see everything with precision, and it is also difficult for the witness to describe that she knows exactly that she was shot at by precisely Milan Lukic. She knows this with precision. But agree with Mr. Groome that in such circumstances and in a state of panic, it is really difficult to register every little detail.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I saw him very well, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going to adjourn now. What we'll do is give you 10 minutes more.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that will be quite enough, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we're going to adjourn. Witness B-1054, don't speak to anybody, please, about your evidence until it's over. And that does include the members of the prosecuting team.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. 1054, in relation to these injuries that you sustained and that you speak about, you attached the discharge paper from the hospital, and I have a copy here.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: With relation to this, I have just a couple of questions. From what I see in the discharge paper -- and you say you were wounded in your left arm and left leg, and you had burns on your arm. From what I see in the letter of discharge, I suppose that Mr. May, Kwon, and Robinson, in view of their profession, know the Latin language well, it says here in the diagnosis: "Wound inflicted by a fragment of the bullet in the shoulder area." That is the first wound indicated, "una slapitaria jonas brak," [phoen] that is the shoulder. And the second one is a multiple fracture of the upper arm, something completely different to what you describe as your wounds. Tell me, finally, how did you, in fact, sustain this injury from a fragment of a bullet in your upper arm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: I did not sustain any other injury than a bullet injury in my left arm. Here, look, if you want to see it. And above the knee, on my left leg, I had an entry and exit wound. Here on my arm is where the bullet came in, and on the other side where it came out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Another thing you say in the statement given to the security centre in Zenica --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I suppose that this letter of discharge has been exhibited. If it hasn't, I would like to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we go on to that, Mr. Groome, have you got that document, the letter of discharge?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, we do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you could produce it, and we'll give it the next exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Next Defence number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit 177, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And again I'd ask that that be under seal since it identifies the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say in this statement that you spent 22 days in the hospital in Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Yes, 22 days. Maybe more. I didn't count. In any case, there was no place where I could lie in, so I went there to be re-bandaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So 22 days or more. In the letter of discharge, however, it says that you spent exactly 10 days there, from the 23rd June, 1992, until the 3rd of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And gentlemen, regardless of whether it has been translated or not, the letter of discharge is very clear because the dates are very legible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How do you explain this discrepancy? Did you make a mistake?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: I couldn't have been mistaken. There are doctors who admitted me on the spot, and they could come here and explain even better than I am doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's what it says here, and you spent not 22 days or more, but ten days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has answered that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the witness did answer. That's not what I'm doubting. I'm doubting the substance of that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. 1054, I want to clarify only one other matter: As far as I can see from these papers, the investigators showed to you the photographs of ten different men for identification purposes so that you can identify the men who allegedly participated in the events you recounted.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Not ten, but the photographs of people who are charged with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just viewing the documents that I have received from Mr. Groome. You say in your brief witness statement, where it says in handwriting "amended on the 21st of July," ERN number 0108792, "The investigator showed me a series of ten photographs -" this is written by you - "marked with numbers from 1 to 10." And in the next paragraph, it says: "You asked me whether I can identify any of the men. My answer is yes. I can identify the man in the picture number 4. It is Mitar Vasiljevic, whom I used to know. He used to be a waiter working at a hotel. I mentioned him earlier in the statement that I have signed."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I knew Mitar very well, and I recognised him from the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you go on to say: "I do not know the men on the other photographs."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: I don't want to say anything about those I don't know. I knew him, and I confirmed his identity.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask you, Mr. May, in view of the fact that this witness was shown ten photographs, out of which she recognised only one as Mitar Vasiljevic, I would kindly ask you to ask Mr. Groome if he could clarify the identity of these other ten persons, because I would very much like to know whether the other nine include any of the men that the witness referred to and allegedly recognised at the time when the events took place, according to her statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll get the Prosecution to do that. You can do it in written form if you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I can simply explain now, if it pleases the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was an identification procedure done to test the witness's ability to identify the perpetrators of this event. The only person -- the only photograph in this series of photographs that has anything to do with this event is number 4, Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic. The other photographs are of people that have absolutely no connection with the events of Visegrad in any way whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Anything else, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in that case, I have only one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. 1054, even if everything had happened as you say it happened, tell me this: In your description of events, nobody from the JNA or Serbia is mentioned. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: I didn't say that anybody from the JNA was there at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you knew all these people that you mentioned, and all those people were from the neighbouring village.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have only one request to make, to avoid misunderstanding. I don't want anyone to think that these casualties are not real. I don't want you to misunderstand me as dealing with that part. That was never my aim, and it is not now. I just want to draw your attention to page 3, paragraph 4, of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the English transcript. In fact, the English version of this witness statement because that's what I would like to start with. Questioned Mr. Tapuskovic:

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Witness, if you could be so kind as to look at page 3 of the statement you gave to the investigators in 1998. Look at what you stated: "On our way to the Red Cross building, we passed by the SUP building. And Grujic and Lipovac told us to go to the Red Cross building. Grujic and Lipovac went into the SUP building and stayed there." Was that how it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is the next sentence, then, true? "So we continued unescorted to the Red Cross building, but there was no one there because it was a Sunday."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you came across some policemen who cursed you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But in the last sentence of that paragraph, you say: "They did not guard us, but all the time they were just passing by, going to and fro." They did not ask anything of you? They didn't say anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: No, they didn't ask anything. It was all in the street under the lindens, the linden trees. The only question was addressed to us by this policeman whom we didn't know. We just said that we were going, and we didn't know where we were going.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, but two paragraphs below. In the middle of that paragraph, it says that you were going along the main street of your neighbourhood towards the houses of Jusuf Memic and Mujo Memic, and the Serb police did not escort you. So you went there unaccompanied. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: They said, "Just go there, nobody would harm you, and you can try to settle there."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But when you came to that house where what you described happened, you said that not a single soldier stayed behind to guard you. And you explained: "We were too frightened to try to leave."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Who would guard us there? They just put us up there. And when they came to loot our houses, they returned to set us on fire. Mitar Lukic and this Mitar Vasiljevic and all the others, I don't want to enumerate them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But on your way to that house where everything else later happened, nothing happened.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: No, not on the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just look at this statement given on the 14th of August, 1995. That is much earlier than this statement given in 1998. Please look at how you described this in this statement, that is, paragraph 3 of that statement. "When we arrived in front of the Red Cross building in Visegrad, the Serb police arrived. Among them I recognised [redacted] [redacted]. They drove us all the way to the Drina bridge." And then you say: "I saw around 150 people, women and children, whom Chetniks were driving to the bridge, and the Chetnik -- a bearded Chetnik around 50 years of age was slaughtering them while the others were throwing them into the water." Is this how it happened, what you saw on that road on your way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Yes, all this happened, but I don't have any more forbearance to go on recounting it. The river was red with blood.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you didn't say this in 1998, and even the other witness who was heard by this Court did not mention this, because if everything happened exactly as you described here, then it is simply impossible for you to have failed to mention this to the OTP investigators.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: I omitted a lot of things because I simply can't stand speaking about them any more. I am overwhelmed by sadness and anguish, and everything is exactly as I stated it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You described that on that day, nobody accompanied you. You said that in 1998 and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has given her explanation, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, she did not give an explanation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not helpful. You've heard what this witness has said. You have pointed out the discrepancy. It will be a matter for us to consider whether there's any significance in it or not. Now, you've carried out your duty. Is there anything more you wish to ask the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, I do have questions. I don't understand your anger. I'm just trying to assist. You should, of course, believe this witness; it's up to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You will not address the Trial Chamber in those words. It is not proper for counsel to use them. You remember your position. Now, you're supposed to be helping this Trial Chamber. The witness has given an explanation for the discrepancy, and you should move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm only trying to be of assistance. I'm not trying to do anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do not continually reply back. Just get on with your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, just a couple of minutes, because I have to pull myself together after this, if you can believe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Here is how you described in your statement of the 12th and 13th of February, 1998, the events involving those two young girls. You said this on page 4, last paragraph. You said that these two girls had been taken away, and when they came back their clothes were in order, only their expressions had changed. You didn't notice anything else about them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: I just said about Jasmina Vila, that she was so full of bite marks, as if she was an eaten potato. And the other two also refused to say any more about what happened when we asked them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But on that occasion, you mentioned only two girls, and you said you hadn't noticed anything in particular about them except that their expressions had changed.
