But when questioned in this earlier case, you mentioned three persons, not two. And on that occasion, you said something different. You said that those two or three persons, when they returned, had their buttons torn off, their clothes were torn - that is on page 1.441 - and you saw bite marks on them. And you also mentioned that they had been taken away and returned after a while. There is a slight difference.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: As for the buttons being torn off, there was a girl who didn't want to take her clothes off herself, so they had to tear them off her.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, explain this, please: In your statement given in the security centre on the 14th of August, you said that what they had gone through, they had gone through in the neighbouring room, and you heard both screams and cries for help, and immediately after that, you were able to see what had happened to them. Those are two different explanations. How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Yes, in the neighbouring room. Jusuf Memic's house was large. I don't even know all the rooms. In one room they put us up in the first place. In another room, they took our valuables away. If I attempted to recount everything in every detail, I would simply break down. I would have to be on medication. That's why I omitted a lot of things. I was trying to tell you the best way I could for the Judges to hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just going to read to you part of what this witness said about what happened in this house, how fire was set on the house in one statement and in another statement given to the officials of this Tribunal. I would like you to explain to the Trial Chamber how come that you learned that your child was alive only after five years?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us consider for a moment what you're doing. Are you suggesting that this witness is not telling the truth? Is that the suggestion, that this incident with the fire and the civilians did not happen? Is that the suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm telling you yet again what I have been saying all along: It is not for me to decide at all; it is for you to assess the validity or invalidity of all statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But what is the point? Let's think for a moment. What is the point? You pointed out some discrepancies in the witness's account. Now, unless it's suggested that this witness was not in the house, that it was not set fire to, and a large number of people were not killed, I'm not sure that we're taken very much further because she has given details in different statements. What is it that you want us to decide in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, really, even if you take action against me that you deem necessary, I have to say that I have been a lawyer for 40 years, and believe me, I'm always in a position to put questions on the basis of which you will assess whether a statement is valid or not. That is not for me to judge. I put questions, and then you are going to assess what this witness says. And I deeply believe that you are going to assess all these facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We know all that. But I'm asking you to consider and explain for a moment how we're assisted by the fact that there are discrepancies in her account. The overall account that this happened has not been challenged by the accused, that these people were in the house, it was set fire to, they were burned. Now, the precise detail of how that happened does not appear at the moment to matter very much. It's not being suggested this witness is not telling the truth about it. So I'd like you to consider, when you're reflecting on what questions you want to ask, not simply to ask because there are discrepancies, but to see if there's any point in the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I have an objection. You say that I did not dispute this. No one in Serbia has ever heard of these events. It is so incredible. People would have had to have heard about this kind of thing if people had been burned down in houses in this way. It's not at the other end of the world; it's in a neighbouring republic. So what does this mean, that I did not challenge it or dispute it? Do we have to -- they have to prove that this happened. It's not for me to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one at a time. We now understand the position, that the accused challenges that this ever occurred at all. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic, ask your questions, but don't, please, take up too much time about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I shall not, Your Honour Judge May. But please take a look at this: The witness spoke about yet another event. She said that she had just heard this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But please, Madam Witness, look at page 7. Before this list that you give, you wrote here, or rather, stated: "After that, in some house in Bikavac, 80 people were put up. [redacted]. I did not see this, but I heard the screaming coming from this house and I smelled the smell in the air coming from the direction of Bikavac." Is it true that in a way, you were the eyewitness of this other group of victims, these 80 victims, that you experienced this, too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Sir, Bikavac and Nova Mahala are not kilometres away. This is a short distance. It's 5 minutes away, if you can put that way, one from each other. And of course 80 people did burn down, 80 souls. And since you claim that this did not happen, there is this glorious court here and let them decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you just explain to the Court how come this kind of list of victims was compiled? I'm not challenging that these people lost their lives, but these names and surnames, how was this list made? Were these bodies first found as of people who had lost their lives, or did you just list these names without knowing whether these people had lost their lives?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: At Adem Omeragic's house where we were burned down, all the names were written down and I identified that in Bikavac. And I did not count them. But Zehra, who is the survivor, this young girl, she can say who was up there. And as for the people who were there with me, there are all the names and surnames listed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just one more thing: Your very own child reappeared safe and sound. Thank goodness that this happened. Now, on the basis of what can we know for sure that all of these people have lost their lives?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: Yes, so you're saying that my son should have lost his life, too?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Heaven forbid, but just, it's possible.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1054
utterances.text: From this house that was burning, I first threw out my son. Two or three minutes after him, I jumped out. So when I was wounded in the left arm and leg, I thought that I had died, that I was killed because I went numb. A few minutes later, I came to, and I realised that I was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. wounded in the arm and leg. So I don't think this is a lie. And a few minutes ago, Mr. Milosevic, what he said, that people in Serbia have never heard of these burnings, then he should look at the cemetery in Potocari and see what happened there. And I think that he's saying that he hasn't even heard of Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I do apologise if there was a misunderstanding, but I truly believe that this is not outside the spirit and the actual job of an amicus curiae. Of course it is for you to assess the facts but it seems to me that these questions should be raised and could be of assistance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Court should then decide --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going to move on now. Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no other questions, but should the Chamber find that the issue with respect to Jasmina Vila, which was raised by both the accused and Mr. Tapuskovic, be an important one, there was other evidence in the case which the Prosecution would be prepared to tender which indicated that she had been the subject of protracted and repeated sexual violence, sexual assaults, by Milan Lukic in the days and weeks preceding her eventual burning to death on this night, and we would be prepared to tender that. With respect to the other fire that now has been called into question, the Prosecution is also prepared to produce --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Tapuskovic, I believe that when you are cross-examining as to discrepancies and the line of cross-examination is such as to suggest that a particular incident did not take place at all and that a witness is fabricating, you should actually put it to the witness very squarely. It's not enough just to cross-examine on the discrepancies. When Mr. Milosevic was cross-examining on discrepancies, I said to myself that that line of cross-examination would only be feasible if he was actually suggesting that the incident did not take place at all. Put it squarely to the witness that the witness is fabricating and let her give a response so that there be no misunderstanding. Because this particular line is really taken from the common law, and that is how it is done. You must put it squarely to the witness that the witness is lying, fabricating, is making up the entire story so that there is no misunderstanding and the witness has a fair chance of responding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We don't need to hear evidence about the side issue which you referred. But the witness should have the chance to answer the question which -- the suggestion which has been made. Witness B-1054, you've heard this discussion, and you've heard what is now suggested by Mr. Milosevic, that he's never heard of this and therefore it never happened. Now, you should have the opportunity to answer that because effectively, what is being said is that you've not told the truth about this house in which these people were and their being killed in the way which you've described. Now, it's suggested that isn't the truth. You should have the opportunity to answer. Did it happen or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this truly happened. But Milosevic did not accept this, whether we were burning, whether we were killed. But it is the truth for sure. So when he claims that it's not true that these people were burned down in this house and that I survived that house, then how come all these people were killed in Potocari, how come there are so many graves and graveyards? He hasn't heard of that either?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. That concludes your evidence, B-1054. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are now free to go. Would you just perhaps until the blinds come down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll recall the earlier witness. This is not a directed witness, is it, this one?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So we can have the blinds up and the screens removed when we have someone to do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: The witness's name is Mr. Josip Josipovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, if you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we concluded the summary yesterday, and I think we are -- Mr. Milosevic is to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday, I got this rather lengthy statement of Mr. Josipovic. I shall go in the right order, but I just want to make an exception at the very beginning. Actually, I would like to quote the very end of the witness statement of Mr. Josipovic because I got the statement in Serbian only yesterday. I had it in the English language. I can say to you that in the statement in the English language, that is the very end of the statement. That is 01067675. And then it continues on page 76. But I'm going to read from the Serbian translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you're going to ask the witness about his statement, he should have a copy of it in his own language. He has got one. Whereabouts in the -- do we have a paragraph number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thirty-six.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: In the second statement, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 36, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If the witness could find that, please. Have you got that? Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So throughout your statement, Mr. Josipovic, you speak about various events that pertain to conflicts between the local population, Serb, Croat, and Muslim. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only the Serb and Croat populations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And then you talked about people being killed in the villages of Bacin, Hrvatska Dubica, Predore, Tanac, Visnjica, Cerovljani, and so on. Is that right, Mr. Josipovic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to read this paragraph out to you, this is paragraph 36. Paragraph 36 of your statement where you say verbatim: "I think that the killing of people in the village of Bacin, Hrvatska Dubica, Predore, Tanac, Visnjica, and Cerovljani were ordered by Stevo Radunovic and Momcilo Kovacevic. They were the commanders, and they were in charge of the Serbs in the region. I know that Milan Martic came from Knin several times and met with Radunovic and Kovacevic. Once when we were collecting livestock, I heard the guards mentioning the name of Milan Martic and that he had arrived with the helicopter that we saw. I heard the guards say that the helicopter had to land in Zivaje. Radunovic and Kovacevic were dismissed when the JNA and the JNA military police took over the area. I think they were dismissed according to Martic's decision. I think the orders to kill people in the area were taken by Radunovic and Kovacevic. When the JNA and the military police took over, the looting and burning stopped." So these persons you consider responsible throughout your statement were dismissed on the basis of Martic's decision, and the army and the military police came. And you yourself say when the JNA and the military police took over, looting and burning stopped. Mr. Josipovic, doesn't this point to the fact that the JNA did everything to stop all violence and to provide security for the citizens themselves and for their property wherever they were?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question. I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you, in view of what you said in your statement, doesn't this confirm that the Yugoslav People's Army, where it came, ensured the safety and security of the citizens and prevented a conflict?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because it had conflicts with the local population, with the Serbs, the Chetniks. And in order to gain power, that's how they acted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume that they acted the way you put it. They were even in conflict with the Serb paramilitary forces in order to stop the conflict between them and you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. And before that, they had helped them, given them weapons and everything. And when they got out of control and they couldn't handle them any longer, then they took all measures to stop them from doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But when you speak about power in the area, you mention that those people that you identified as being responsible were replaced by a decision of Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my opinion, and that was what I thought at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who else could have replaced them if they belonged to the Serbian army of Krajina, or the police of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just referring to your own statement that they were replaced by Martic. But let us go back to the beginning of the questions that I have for you. You stated at the very beginning of your statement that before the elections, relations were normal between Serbs and Croats in Croatian Hrvatska Dubica. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in that same paragraph, you say that after the elections, the Croats won a large majority and immediately after that formed the National Guards Corps. Is that right, a military unit?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't have time to highlight and mark the documents I received yesterday, so I made my notes on the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says here: "Hrvatska Dubica was a small town with mixed population, but with a slight majority [In English] of Croats living there. After the elections in 1990, the HDZ party got a great majority in the elections. Shortly after, the Croats formed a national guard called Zenga. Zenga had a military structure. The Serbs had the Territorial Defence. This was a reserve force for JNA that had been existing for many years. The Croats that were in the Territorial Defence left in 1990 after the elections. Before the elections, there were normal relations between Croats and Serbs in the village. "From the moment when the Zenga was established, the relations between the Serbs and Croats in the village changed. There was a lack of trust, and nobody felt safe any more." [Interpretation] And so on. So my question to you was after the Croats won a major majority at the elections, they formed a National Guards Corps, a military structure. You said that was not so, and I have just quoted what you yourself said. So was that right or not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the breakup of the former Yugoslavia, as Croats wanted an Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. independent Croatia, it was normal for them to set up Croatian power and a Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking you, Mr. Josipovic, what is normal in your opinion. I'm asking you in connection with what you said. In 1990, immediately after the elections you formed a virtually paramilitary unit called the National Guards Corps. Though you don't call it that, that is up to you. But my point is that you immediately formed the National Guards Corps as a military entity immediately after the elections. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. And had Croatia lost this war, it would be a paramilitary unit. But Croatia won this war, it won its own state, and recognition of that state. Therefore, it was not paramilitary police or army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is common knowledge under what circumstances you were recognised. But in any event, when this was happening in 1990, things were quite different. Mr. Josipovic, prior to that, you were doing your military service in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You know very well what a military structure means.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in 1990, the National Guards Corps was formed as some sort of a party army. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't put it like that, that it was an army of a party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, is it right that at the time Croatia was a republic within the still-existing SFRY at the time you formed the National Guards Corps?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was part of it, but it wanted to secede from the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that the Serbs at the time had the Territorial Defence as a reserve force of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In what I quoted, it follows that it was no Serbian Territorial Defence but it was the right and duty of all citizens of the SFRY, of the citizens living in the area, and the TO was composed of both Serbs and Croats; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But when the National Guards Corps began to be formed, the Croats started abandoning the TO and switched over to the National Guards Corps. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as they no longer trusted the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did the Serbs in the area of Hrvatska Dubica have any kind of army at the time which would be some sort of army of theirs?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What kind of army?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Chetnik band gangs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you said that there was the Territorial Defence which belonged to all citizens, and that the Croats abandoned it and crossed over to the National Guards Corps.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the former Yugoslavia, it was of all citizens, and everyone was in the TO. But as everything collapsed and due to various developments that occurred, it was normal for the Croats no longer to be suitable for the TO and the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean they were not "suitable"?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't want to be in the TO and the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone expel them from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did, and they threatened and they were in jeopardy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of anyone who was thrown out of the JNA because he was a Croat?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say on page 7 -- actually paragraph 7, page 2, that from the moment the Zenga was established, there was a lack of trust in the area of Hrvatska Dubica among the population.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That Serbs during the night crossed the Una to spend the night in Bosnia and would come back to their homes in the morning. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the evening they would go because they were afraid of what -- because what they had done on the other side of the Una River. And then during the day they would return, to feel safe, like the other Serbs who normally stayed on to spend the night in Hrvatska Dubica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They went away during the night not to be liquidated during the night. They would spend the night on the Bosnian side and during the day they would come back to work, they were peasants, farmers, they had to take care of their farming work.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. They went to join the JNA, their tanks and Howitzers to open fire on their own Serbs, they really went there to get information and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Josipovic, are you trying to tell us now, even though you stated something quite different in your statement, that some Serbs during the night would cross the Una to spend the night in Bosnia to open fire on their own Serbs on this side of the river?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm saying, Mr. Milosevic, because that's how it was essentially. When the Serbs went to the other side of the Una, those who stayed behind were told to hide in basements and in other places so that those who crossed the Una would be able to fire on us and the whole population. And in some cases when a Serb was injured, normally they would say that the Ustashas had done it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But you formed, immediately after the elections, the National Guards Corps. The Serbs fled during the night to sleep in Bosnia, fearing that they would be killed during the night, and now you're saying that the Serbs were crossing the river to open fire on you and other Serbs on the other bank of the river.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. So that's what you claim. That's very fine. Now, what were the Serbs afraid of to make them cross the Una to Bosnia to leave their homes unprotected?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You will have to ask them that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Josipovic, in paragraph 8 on page 2, you say that the situation changed dramatically after the Territorial Defence, that is, the Serbs, arrested eight men, among whom you knew two; Tomislav Mateljak, and Predrag Vucicevic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mateljak was a Croat, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was. And this Vucicevic, he too was a Croat and still is a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't doubt that, that if he was a Croat then, that he is still a Croat. And Mateljak, as you yourself say, in those days was the commander of the National Guards Corps. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that you know, and that it was known then, too, that Mateljak was a criminal?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that at the time. I just know that he was an orphan and that he was brought up by his grandmother.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say - and this is the last paragraph on page 1 of your statement, I have the English version here: [In English] "Mateljak is a criminal." "I consider Mateljak as a criminal. I know that Mateljak was unemployed before the war. He was a tramp, and he lived in a small ruined house in Cerovljani. However, after the party HDZ was founded, he suddenly became a very powerful and rich person." [Interpretation] So this is what you wrote, Mr. Josipovic. How come you're now telling us that you didn't know that he was a criminal, but you wrote this, that he was a tramp? I had never heard of Mateljak; I never heard of you either before I received your statement.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not true. I didn't write that. I just gave a statement to that effect, my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But I assume they noted down what you said.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they noted down what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's quite sufficient, then. Who technically actually wrote it down is not important; the important thing is that that was your opinion.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So Mr. Josipovic, a local criminal became the commander of the local National Guards Corps. And as you say, when he came into power, he became a very powerful and rich person in the HDZ. How do you explain that fact?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My explanation is that the authorities at the time should have needed people of that kind, and more such people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As he was such a person you yourself describe as a criminal and a tramp, does it mean that the fear of the Serbs from that type of armed unit, with a commander who was a criminal, such as this Mateljak was, was justified, that it was justifiable that the Serbs should fear such an armed grouping under the command of such a criminal, even in your own opinion? Is that so, Mr. Josipovic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't. One cannot say that it was justified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So their fear was not justified, despite all these facts that you yourself have given?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had no need to fear anything. Regardless of the fact that I consider him to be that, and because he did behave in that way and because he was such a man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he behaved in that way and was such a man, and he was in charge of this armed formation, yet, in your opinion, the Serbs had no reason to fear such a formation with such a commander?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I didn't say that he was a murderer and a criminal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell us now, to what extent were Serbs indeed terrorised by a criminal such as Mateljak?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not exposed to any kind of terror at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Nothing was done against them?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing. Absolutely nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say that Vucicevic was the second person who was arrested and that you knew. And on page 3, paragraph 2, you said that Mateljak managed to get away and that Vucicevic was later on exchanged. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So neither of them, although one was a criminal and another a newly recruited member of the MUP of Croatia, came to any harm. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. With the proviso that he was shown on TV showing what the Serb Chetniks and JNA troops had done to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All of them together, Serb Chetniks, and the JNA, what did they do to him?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am still unclear about this today, who was Serbian Chetnik, what was JNA, what was TO, and what were Martic's men, and whether they were under the command of the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you are still unclear about this, I hope you understand that absolute chaos reigned at that time.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but there were commanders of all these formations. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So who were the commanders?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I certainly didn't, if you did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Josipovic. But tell me, what did Vucicevic do before he became chief of the MUP of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the following paragraph, paragraph 3 on page 3, you state that local Serbs, as you call them, were active in the region. All of them, you say, were local Serbs, and they wore the same olive-green uniforms of the JNA. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So is it true, since you had done your military service just before that, that all members of the reserve force of the JNA, or at least the majority of them, regardless of which republic - Serbia, Bosnia, Croatia, or some other republic - they were from, you know that all of them had drawn these uniforms from the supply of the JNA and they kept them at home so that when called up they could put them on and report to their units?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some of the men had uniforms. I didn't because I wasn't issued with one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You did not do your military service?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You did not have a wartime assignment in the reserve force?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But those who, as reservists or members of the TO, had uniforms, does it mean, just the fact that they had uniforms after being discharged from the army or the TO, does it mean they were members of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they wore the star, the emblem of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When it started, they simply put on these uniforms that they had kept at home?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see any reason why they would put on these uniforms if you say yourself that Croats and Muslims had the same uniforms. Why didn't the Croats and Muslims put them on?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Because they had a different attitude probably towards the JNA and Yugoslavia. That's one thing. And another thing, I would not like to lump everybody together because there were different Croats and Muslims who stayed in the JNA and even occupied the highest posts. You know that too, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On paragraph 3 on page 3, you say after saying these local Serbs were your neighbours, naming them, which means that those were people whom you knew. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were any of them a member of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday when asked about this, you said some of them were local Serbs and others were from Bosnia and Herzegovina. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But those from Bosnia-Herzegovina, I suppose they had come from nearby places across the Una River. None of them were from very distant parts.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were also people from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't mention anyone from Serbia. Who did you see from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't mention it because I wanted to be brief, to make this procedure brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But do you have a single name for a person who allegedly came from Serbia, and where they came from exactly?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not in a position to find out. But there were a couple of them who were bragging that they were from Serbia, how they were involved in Vukovar and how they had come to take their revenge, to repay a debt from the Second World War, against me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you can't tell me a single name.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even if I had known it then, I couldn't possibly recall it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me just clarify something. When did you meet or come across the couple who were bragging that they were from Serbia and they were involved in Vukovar? When was it that you came across those two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I was taken captive. I think it was in October 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in October 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How was it possible in October 1991 for anyone to tell you they were involved in Vukovar? You know that Vukovar fell sometime end of November 1991.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. That's what they told me. They were bragging.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As a matter of accuracy, the siege began in August 1991. So it might have been possible for somebody to talk about Vukovar at the time. Of course, it didn't fall, as the evidence is, until November, but the witness can only say what he saw, what he heard.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, all right, Mr. May. I can't imagine who it could have been, what happened in Vukovar to talk about on the part of the Serbian side or the part of JNA before October. You should know that. You have followed evidence on these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say all of them wore a patch "SAO Krajina" on their sleeve.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they all wore different emblems, whatever they could lay their hands on. Some wore Serbian cockades, others wore patches of the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a certain Sarac who told you he was from Bosanska Dubica.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From around Bosanska Dubica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This place is next to Croatian Dubica, near the other side of the Una River, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is there even a kilometre between the Croatian Dubica and Bosanska Dubica?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not even a kilometre. It is on different sides of the Una River.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you say people from Bosnia-Herzegovina, you were talking about your immediate, your next-door neighbours practically?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I just said there were some neighbours, but there were people from more distant places, like Banja Luka, to mention one. Nedzad, and all the other neighbouring places from Prijedor, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But it's all from the immediate vicinity?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within 80 kilometres, let's say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's move on, Mr. Josipovic. The second person you mention as not being from Dubica either was allegedly from Vukovar. That's the one you mentioned a second ago. Right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. He bragged that his brother was killed in Vukovar, that he had come from Vukovar and that he had come to take revenge for his brother. He said the Ustashas had killed his brother during the conquest of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So again, you are talking about a Serb from Vukovar who was a refugee from Vukovar, not anyone else.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he said he was from Serbia. He had fought together with his brother who was killed in Vukovar, and most probably both he and his brother were from Serbia. I didn't say he was from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you came across him in October, as you say.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly which month it was. I think it could have been October, maybe the end of October. At that time, I didn't keep track even of months, let alone days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, all right, Mr. Josipovic. We don't need that sort of correction. This Serb whom you mention in paragraph 4 ordered a Croatian elderly woman to be buried, and she had died of starvation because nobody attended to her in her village.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose he died of -- she died of starvation. I didn't see any injuries on her, no signs of bullet wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was bad about his helping to have this woman buried?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing that was bad is that, while we were digging the grave for that old woman, when we were inside the pit, he was pushing the rifle barrel into our mouths and he was hitting us with the rifle butt on the head, and he asked us whether we would like to be killed inside that pit and stay inside or bury the old woman first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what you say, but from what I can see, you are alive and well and he didn't kill you inside that pit.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we said we would like to stay alive, we would like to bury that old woman and stay alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Josipovic. How long were you with the National Guards Corps?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About two months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Judging by your statement, you did not join up voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I was unfit for service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who was it that recruited you despite your will into the National Guards Corps?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I joined up myself because I had to, since I wasn't able to go to work, and the only way for me to stay employed and not to get dismissed was to join up with the National Guards Corps. And by virtue of that, I got a certificate allowing me to come back to work eventually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where did you work?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Sisak on Croatia railways, the former Yugoslav railways.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you would not have been able to keep your employment if you had not joined up the National Guards Corps; you would have been dismissed?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right because I wasn't able to travel, I wasn't able to go to work; we were under siege. The war was going on. The only way was to join up with the National Guards Corps. That was the only way I could keep my employment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say here: "In the end of June 1991, my brother, Dragan, cousin Mico Coric and myself went to Kutina. [In English] We were not members of HDZ, and we did not want to fight with anybody. We stayed in a hotel in Kutina. The Croatian police found us and instructed us to go back to Hrvatska Dubica. They told us that we had to join the National Guard Corps Zenga." [Interpretation] So it means that the police in Kutina instructed you that you had to join the National Guards Corps, and you would not have been able to keep your employment if you had failed to do that.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. After Dvor na Uni and Kostajnica were taken, we had to leave because we were afraid of being caught up in the winds of war. And we fled with the rest of the population and we ended up in this hotel in Kutina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, is it true that in the headquarters of the National Guards Corps, you were issued with a weapon, and then you were sent to a bridge between Croatian Dubica and Bosnian Dubica?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was later. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On that bridge, did you link up with the Croatian police who were searching everybody crossing the bridge for weapons or anything else?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then you were under the direct command of this Tomislav Mateljak. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Josipovic, how many fighting men in total were then under the command of this Mateljak man?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know the number of the unit that you belonged to?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had no insight into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The time has come to adjourn. Mr. Josipovic, would you be back, please, in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Josipovic, on page 4 in paragraph 1 of your statement you say that Mateljak issued you with a sniper rifle since, as you say, you were trained in the JNA as a sniper. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was a sniper shooter in the JNA. And Mateljak did give me a sniper rifle, the hunting version of the sniper rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But as I see, you were -- this weapon was taken back from you very soon after that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what was the name of the officer of the Croatian police who ordered you to shoot at the Serbs on the other bank of the river who were observing in your direction?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The Serbs you were supposed to shoot at, according to that order, were they opening fire or were they just observing?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were observing and they were shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see that your orders were to shoot at the people who were observing your side.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose so. That's how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 4, paragraph 2, you stated that a couple of days later, you were informed that a house of a Serb in your village, Stojan Bekic, was burning.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then you went to your village to see what was going on. So tell me, who set Stojan Bekic's house on fire?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You don't even mention in your statement the name of the person who set the house on fire, but you say that the villagers told you that JNA helicopters landed in the vicinity of his house.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the vicinity of his house, but in the vicinity of our houses in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So your houses. It had nothing to do with the house of the Stojan Bekic which was set on fire?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who set it on fire, but most probably there was no connection between the two things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the house was set on fire just because it was Serbian. Right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who set it on fire and whether it is and was a Serb's house. I couldn't answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did you, with your own eyes, see these JNA helicopters on any one occasion?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I came to the village once or twice to visit my parents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, as you say, the villagers told you that the helicopters unloaded some weapons that were transported by a truck belonging to the Elektra company to Zivaja and Sas villages. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's what you were told by the people who lived in the village?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was their opinion. And later on, I went to check out for myself and I did check out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you say you found out what was going on, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The helicopter landed in the woods along the road where vehicles and smaller freight vehicles were parked. I saw weapons being unloaded, and all the other stuff. And behind the helicopter, they were unloaded on to -- they were loaded on to vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you didn't see where those weapons were taken?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know in which direction they were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the direction of these villages that I mentioned?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what kind of weapons did you see?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw automatic weapons, because the Serbs who had come to pick the weapons up opened these trunks and took the best weapons for themselves, the new weapons. And the rest they loaded on to vehicles. On that occasion, I could see that the contents of the trunks were weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How much approximately?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, approximately four or five vehicles loaded with weapons, maybe 50 to 70 cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me something about this train. You mention a train which was coming from the direction of Novska. And fire was opened from the train on Serbs from 50 and 60 millimetre cannons.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The train was using the railroad towards Bosanska Dubica, and I was passing by carrying food supplies, driving food supplies to the village. I stopped by to talk to friends and asked them, "What is this train doing here?" And they told me: "Of course, they are shooting at Serbs. They are defending. Dubica had fallen, and it is occupied by Serbs." So they were covering the people who were withdrawing and the troops who were withdrawing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you saw the shooting from this train?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that. I only saw the train.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you saw the weapons on the train?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was something hand-made, done at the iron works, maybe five or six hand-made mortars without the full set of equipment. It was hand-held by one man while another was shooting. Other people were pushing in shells. And they had some sort of improvised aiming device. It was ridiculous to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Also, is it correct that the Croat forces during the night between the 13th and 14th September, 1991, destroyed the bridge that linked Bosanska and Hrvatska Dubica?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, and it was destroyed in order to stop the JNA from crossing the river. And they didn't want the JNA to come in with their armoured vehicles and weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who issued the order to destroy the bridge?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I understand, from this statement of yours, on the following day, on the 15th of September, you were arrested. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know all the persons who were arrested with you on that day?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many of you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my village, all the people who happened to be there were arrested. Perhaps it was about ten persons or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you spoke about eight persons.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said eight. But it's the same thing, eight or ten. I didn't count them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who arrested you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb army, the JNA arrested us. The Martic people. I don't know. The TO. Whoever. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that the TO from your village there?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The TO was registered as if it were from my village, but under whose command they were, something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know these people who arrested you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew some. I didn't know others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They knew you, and you knew them?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, the one you gave on the 5th of September, 1992, in the municipality of Hrvatska Kostajnica, you stated that on that day you were arrested by, as you put it, the local Chetniks, Mico Tepic, Vaso Paukovic, a certain Rajko. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Those are the names of the persons who I knew. And those are the persons who I did mention, whose names I mentioned and everything. I those didn't know, I didn't mention, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that on that occasion, they interrogated you about the weapons that you had and about the positions where the members of the ZNG were?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. That is correct, too. But before that, they took five or six of us to be a human shield in front of them so that they would go to the Sava River in order to reconnoiter to see where the positions of the Croat army and the Croat MUP was, they had put it. And then on that occasion, they asked us how many Croatian troops were there, how many Croatian policemen were there and so on and so forth. And then I said when we came to the Sava River, "You can see yourselves how long the village is. It's perhaps 3 kilometres or 3 and a half kilometres long. You can see how populated it is, and you can see how many people there are there." I did not know how many people there were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was my understanding that in that village, as for the local population, they only arrested you and Mico Coric. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That was after they returned from this reconnaissance mission because we were a human shield, as I said. The rest were left alone, and they took us away. They took them away later, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 6, in paragraph 2, you say that while you were in captivity, you were forced to repair the bridge. I assume that this is the bridge between Hrvatska Dubica and Bosanska Dubica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it correct that in addition to you, who were taken prisoner, local Serbs also took part in repairing the bridge?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, people who were convicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They were also arrested, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were arrested or taken into custody for forced labour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You called them convicts.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I called them. That is the name I used for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In the statement you gave in Hrvatska Kostajnica you stated that Antun Knezevic and Zeljko Abaza from Bacin were killed while you were detained in the old school Dubicanka [phoen] in Hrvatska Dubica. Is that right? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But I didn't see in your statement, the statement to the investigators of the Tribunal, that you mention anywhere the way in which they were killed.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe it's an error that slipped through, but there must be an explanation of that killing and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Nowhere in your statement to the investigators did you mention that Abaza -- Knezevic had his throat slit as you stated on the 5th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether they slit his throat or killed him, when they forced us to load them on, when we came to, the first thing I noticed was that his throat had been slit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you didn't see them actually being killed, or how, nor by whom.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true; I didn't see who killed them, how they killed them, or with what, nor what happened to them. But afterwards, when I regained consciousness, because they had probably been killed after I fainted -- they hit me on the head with a metal pole, I fell and lost consciousness. From there on, I don't know what happened. But when I regained consciousness, when they poured cold water on us, then I saw what had happened to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then sometime around Christmas, you were in prison. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who ran the prison? Who was in control?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the JNA that had taken over from the locals and the TO. Simply, they replaced them. The JNA took over control and replaced the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see, so when the JNA came, they replaced them. And this is linked to the paragraph I quoted from at the beginning, because when the JNA arrived, there was no further mistreatment, was there?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, there was no mistreatment after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that it was upon the insistence of the Serb, Stojan Bekic, whose house had been torched in your village, Predore, that you were transferred to Prijedor from where, 25 days later, you were transferred to Banja Luka. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd rather not talk about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any particular reason for not wanting to talk about it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us about it in private session?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I didn't want to talk about it. I don't wish to mention Mr. Stojan Bekic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, I won't insist. Did anyone mistreat you in Prijedor or Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards mistreatment, no one mistreated me until they found out who and what I was. As soon as they learned about that, because I was in the barracks in a dormitory where convicts were held who had fled from Lipik, Daruvar, and Novska, and they were with me together and they started talking, and through the conversation as to who we were, where we were from and what we were doing, that is how they learned I was a Croat and what I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And they didn't know that before that, when you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no one knew, none of the officers knew that I was such and such a person. And that was the reason. Nor did they know why I had got there, why I had come to the barracks in Prijedor. Later on when they found out who I was and what I was, I was transferred to the guards' room, again some kind of military detention for soldiers where they intimidated me. They tried to frighten me, but nobody beat me or mistreated me or touched me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At any point in time during the events that you are describing, did you see a soldier or officer of the JNA mistreating anyone?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did see JNA soldiers. Actually, I was mistreated in Prijedor. Well, not really mistreated, just threatened behind a closed door. They would beat on the door with their truncheons, with their belts, and other such nonsense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They were banging on the door of the detention unit?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the detention area where I was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But when the JNA arrived, all the torching, looting, and unlawful action ceased. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one could say so, more or less. One could say that the authorities had arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, on the 7th to the 11th of March, 2002, you made an additional statement to the investigators.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't remember this additional statement?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I don't know what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me just try and find it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I took note of it somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is part of the 92 bis package, yes, indeed. The starting ERN number I have is 02167694.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see this now. 76... At any rate, there is an additional statement, as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is about a year after you gave your first statement; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe it is so. Most probably it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of this additional statement, you say that you gave it of your own free will, and I wish you to explain it to me. Did you yourself decide to give this additional statement, or did they ask you to give an additional statement?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I decided myself to give this supplementary statement, because when I was first asked to give a statement for The Hague Tribunal, I was working in the meantime, and I didn't have time. So I wanted this to happen as soon as possible. I wanted it to be as brief as possible, too. I wanted to finish as soon as possible, that's what I'm trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, in this first statement, you did not mention that these people who you accuse of having been responsible for that, Radunovic and Kovacevic, that they acted on orders coming from Mile Martic. As a matter of fact, in paragraph 36, the one I quoted to you from the first statement, it is quite obvious that Mile Martic replaced those two men. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the objective of Milan Martic. Most probably they were replaced. However, since they did not want to be replaced, I don't believe that he managed to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you yourself said that they were dismissed by him.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were dismissed, but then they came back to power a day or two later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, so he came and he dismissed them, and then they came back to these positions a day or two later; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they were not working on his orders, at least that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know on whose orders they were acting, his or the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you must bring your examination to an end because you're over time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I'm going to bring it to an end now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand this because you gave this supplementary statement by the time I had been accused here. At whose initiative did you give this statement?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whose initiative it was. At any rate, I gave it voluntarily, this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You, yes, highlight that, that you give it voluntarily. Tell me, did you give this statement by way of some kind of free interpretation or did somebody put questions to you and did you then answer these questions?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course questions were put to me and I answered these questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, so they put questions to you and you answered them.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. But I mentioned that during the first statement I didn't have enough time, that my time was very short then, and I could not say everything during that first statement. I couldn't describe everything that happened to me within those five months, and I got only an hour away from work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in that first statement, you say that they were doing something on the orders of Milan Martic, and that Milan Martic dismissed them.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josipovic, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, I'm going to be very, very brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Josipovic, I would like to draw your attention to paragraphs 12 and 13 of your statement. I don't know whether I heard this. Perhaps I missed something. You speak of the month of June 1991 there. Have you found it? You speak of the month of June. And in paragraph 13 you say, "We were told to go to headquarters, to report at headquarters."

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether you were asked about this, that you were given some old weapons, M48 rifles, in the month of June.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you get these rifles in June?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. Because there weren't any.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But here you said that you did get rifles.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I did get rifles, but the rifles were hunting rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, so they were not M48 rifles?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it was a hunting rifle that had been transformed into a M48, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you were not given uniforms, and you say, "I think that all the members of the HDZ had uniforms then." Does that mean that some civilians were armed too, in addition to the people who belonged to the HDZ then in the month of July?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Those who were perhaps a bit more active, those from the HDZ, of course, and those who were closer. The HDZ, et cetera, of course they had equipment and weapons and uniforms and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Court why this was necessary in the month of June?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. And here in paragraph 17, so then that is the following page, you stated: "Mateljak ordered that the civilian population be evacuated from Hrvatska Dubica and the surrounding villages. This came from President Tudjman. The villagers were very scared and all civilians left." Is that the way you put it then?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said then, and that's what I'm saying now. The reason for that was that Croatia, the Croatian police rather, and the Croatian army, the members of the National Guards Corps did not have sufficient manpower to defend the Croatian Dubica, Hrvatska Dubica. They kept this for themselves. They had to leave, they had to withdraw. And the very few troops they had were just there to secure the retreat of the civilian population until the JNA came in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So in order to carry out certain military operations the civilian population was order to leave that village?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Orders were given for the civilians to withdraw because, of course, the Croatian army, the Croatian police could no longer keep up the defence, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were these people of Croat ethnicity who left these -- this area on those orders?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were Croats and Muslims. There were a few Muslims. There were some Serbs, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Mr. Josipovic, when Mr. Milosevic asked you about the dismissal of Radunovic and Kovacevic by Martic, did you make any personal direct objections how Martic dismissed those two persons?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When Martic wanted to dismiss these two criminals, he simply didn't dare come to Hrvatska Dubica to dismiss them. At the railway Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. station in Hrvatska Dubica, that's where the people who told me who were with me at the farm, they had to stop there, and actually he was taken to Zivaja. And that's where JNA headquarters were, or rather TO headquarters, of Martic, of the army, of the police. I don't know, I'm not sure. But those were the instructions that were given then in Zivaja, that I don't know. And that these two in Hrvatska Dubica should be replaced.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object to the question put by Ms. Bauer. Actually, I have the English version here. The witness says very clearly: "[In English] Martic's decision that they were dismissed."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it is quite undisputable on the basis of his statement that Martic dismissed these people who did not act in accordance with the rules that were part of legality. I think that this speaks in Martic's favour. And I showed you that it was only in the second statement, later, that this witness first mentioned that they allegedly worked on some kind of instructions given by Martic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Listen, it's his evidence which counts. It's not counsel's questions or your objections. Now, he has given his evidence about this, and that's what we'll have to rely on. Yes, I wonder if the registrar would come up, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right, Mr. Milosevic, but Momcilo Kovacevic and Stevo Radunovic while they obeyed Martic everything was fine, but as soon as they got out of his control, he had them dismissed because they had become disobedient and arrogant, and that's why he dismissed them. And that's why I gave my opinion, that I think that is most probably why he dismissed them. That is my explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Bauer.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: At the time he was dismissed, you were in detention. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: So you came about -- who told you about the dismissal of Radunovic and Kovacevic, who were the persons?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These persons were members of the JNA. It was the JNA army.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: And you personally, did they tell you in addition what the reason was and did you give the reasons in an addendum to both statements about two months ago?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Could you say just in one sentence what was the reason these Serb soldiers told you to dismiss Radunovic and Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason was that they had become disobedient, and most probably because they had killed civilian population. Another reason was Zeljko Abaza and Antun Knezovic , when they killed them, they should not have killed them. They were supposed to be exchanged allegedly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Was Jovo Misljenovic as president somewhere involved in this matter or did you hear about his involvement?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC [Resumed]
